method_card.title: Factorising \(ax^2 + bx + c\) (a \neq 1)
steps: Multiply \(a \times c\) to get a target product.
Find two numbers that multiply to \(ac\) and add to \(b\).
Split the middle term \(bx\) into those two terms.
Factorise in pairs and take out the common bracket.
method_card.content: When \(a \neq 1\) you cannot just find two numbers that multiply to \(c\); aim for the product \(ac\). This is the ac method, or splitting the middle term. Rewrite \(bx\) as those two terms, factorise in pairs, then pull out the shared bracket. Always expand your answer to check it gives the original quadratic.
method_card.example:
Factorise \(2x^2 + 5x + 3\)

\(ac = 6\); two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3. Split: \(2x^2 + 2x + 3x + 3 = 2x(x+1) + 3(x+1)\). Answer: \((2x+3)(x+1)\).

bronze.hint: Work out ac = 2 × 3 = 6, then find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.

misconceptions.message: This is \(a \neq 1\), so the simple method fails; multiply \(a \times c\) first, then find the factor pair.
The two numbers must multiply to \(ac\), not just \(c\), and add to \(b\); recompute \(ac\) and pick the right pair.

problem_bank.bronze_description: Factorise quadratics with small, all-positive coefficients.
problem_bank.silver_description: Include negative terms and mixed signs.
problem_bank.gold_description: Larger numbers, perfect squares, and the difference of two squares.

bronze.title: Bronze: factorising with small positive numbers
steps: Multiply a by c (the number in front of \(x^2\) times the constant). This is your target product.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to the middle number b. With all-positive terms both numbers are positive.
Split the middle term into those two pieces, then factorise in pairs to reveal the shared bracket.

steps.label: Factor pair
steps.content: Two numbers multiply to 10 and add to 11: \(10\) and \(1\).

silver.title: Silver: factorising with negative terms
steps: Multiply a by c as before, but watch the sign: a negative constant makes the product negative.
Find two numbers that multiply to that product and add to b. A negative product means one number is positive and one is negative.
Split the middle term and factorise in pairs, keeping every sign as you go.

gold.title: Gold: large products and special cases
steps: Multiply a by c. With larger leading numbers the product can be big, so list the factor pairs carefully.
Pick the pair that multiplies to \(ac\) and adds to b, choosing signs so both come out right, then split, group and check.
Spot the special cases: no middle term is the difference of two squares \(a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)\); a matching pair like \(-6, -6\) gives a perfect square.

steps.hint: The two sides multiply to the area, 12, so the partner of 3 is 12 ÷ 3.

steps.say: You just found two numbers from a target product (12) and a target sum (7). That hunt is the whole engine of factorising \(ax^2+bx+c\): the product you aim for is \(a \times c\), and the sum you aim for is the middle number \(b\). The rest is splitting and bracketing.
When the number in front of \(x^2\) is not 1, use the ac method. First multiply that front number, \(a\), by the constant, \(c\).
Now find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to the middle number, 13.

steps.hint: Add 12 and 1; it should equal the middle number.
steps.done: They hit 12 and 13, so 12 and 1 are the numbers.
